title: Exam Week
subtitle: Ten weeks of Philippine history, one paper.
objectives: Recall the road to independence, 1934 to 1941
Recall the occupation and the return, 1942 to 1945
Recall the presidents and martial law, 1946 to 1986

cards.title: Ten weeks of Philippine history, one paper
cards.text: Twenty-four questions. The review below is grouped by thread, not by week, because that is how the paper will mix them.

cards.title: The road out, 1934 to 1941
cards.text: A ten-year countdown with a war in the middle of it.
points: **Tydings-McDuffie Act, 1934**: independence promised in ten years.
**Commonwealth, 1935**: Quezon president, self-rule in most things.
**National Defense Act, 1935** and a national language chosen.
**December 1941**: the countdown is interrupted.

question.text: The Tydings-McDuffie Act set a transition of…
question.explain: Ten years, which made 1945 the target.

cards.title: Occupation and return, 1942 to 1945
cards.text: Three years of occupation, then a brutal liberation.
points: **Bataan fell in April 1942**; Corregidor in May.
**The Second Republic, 1943**, under Jose P. Laurel.
**Guerrilla resistance** operated throughout.
**Leyte, October 1944**; Manila destroyed in February 1945.

question.text: The Second Republic of 1943 governed independently of Japan.
question.explain: It governed under Japanese authority. That is why its standing is still argued about.

cards.title: Independence with conditions, 1946
points: **4 July 1946**: the Third Republic.
**The Bell Trade Act** tied the peso to the dollar and gave parity rights.
**The Military Bases Agreement, 1947**: 99 years, later cut.
**Parity needed a constitutional amendment** to pass.

cards.title: Conditions attached to a reward
cards.text: You finish the mission and the reward unlocks — with a modifier you did not choose.
points: **Independence was the reward.**
**Parity rights and the bases** were the modifiers.
**Accepting them** was the price of reconstruction money.
**Later governments spent decades** removing them.

cards.title: Presidents and martial law, 1946 to 1986
cards.text: Six presidents, one land problem, and 1972.
points: **Roxas, Quirino, Magsaysay**: rebuilding, corruption, the Huk settlement.
**Garcia's Filipino First**; Macapagal moves Independence Day to 12 June.
**Marcos elected 1965**, re-elected 1969.
**Proclamation 1081, 1972**; EDSA ends it in 1986.

question.explain: Congress was abolished and the press was shut or taken over.

cards.title: How to work the paper
cards.text: Twelve rounds, not one punch. Pace it.
points: **Read the whole question** before touching an option.
**Mark the hard one and move on.** Come back.
**Do not change an answer** without a reason you can say.

cards.title: The night before is part of the exam
cards.text: This is not about being clever on the day.
points: **Sleep beats cramming.**
**Eat something.** Your brain runs on glucose.
**Self-test, do not re-read.** Re-reading feels like learning.
**Five dates, four threads.** That is the whole paper.

cards.title: The four threads
points: 1934 to 1941: a promised countdown, interrupted.
1942 to 1945: occupation, resistance, destruction.
1946: sovereignty with economic and military conditions.
1946 to 1986: land, presidents, martial law, EDSA.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 11 Social Studies, the practice paper. Twenty-four questions spread across all ten teaching weeks, with the review cards grouped by thread rather than by week because the paper mixes them: the promised countdown, the occupation, the conditions attached to 1946, and the presidents through to EDSA. The last review card reduces the term to five dates, which is the smallest thing worth memorising. Exam technique gets its own lens card rather than a sidebar, since pacing a paper is the skill most likely to cost him marks he already knows.
discussion: Which five dates would you keep if you could keep only five?
Can you say what each condition of 1946 actually allowed?
extension: Sit the quiz once at pace, then again days later without revising.
Say each thread aloud in four sentences.
misconceptions: That revision means re-reading rather than self-testing.
That the dates matter more than what happened.
